procedural_history.originating_court: Magistrate Court (implied, as a first information report was lodged and accused were remanded to police custody by a Magistrate)
procedural_history.impugned_order: The High Court held all the three respondents guilty of contempt of court and convicted them accordingly. The High Court imposed a sentence of fine of Rs. 200/- on the first respondent and of administering an admonition to respondents 2 and 3.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A first information report was lodged on Sept. 11, 1967 regarding the loss of life of a person when two groups of people clashed. On Sept, 20, 1967 the first appellant made a statement charging one of the groups being guilty of deliberate conspiracy to commit the murder and alleging that a prominent member of that party had given instructions for this. The respondent along with his two brothers was arrested on Sept . .23, 1967 and on the next day the Magistrate remanded the accused to police custody. In its issue dated Sept. 23. 1967 a newspaper of which the second appellant was the editor printed the statement of the first appellant. Later on all the three accused were produced before the Magistrate. The respondent filed a petition under ss. 3 and ·4 of the Contempt of Court's Act, l 952 against the first appellant, second appellant and the printer of the newspapers. The High Court found all the persons guilty of contempt of court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants A. K. Gopalan and P. Govinda Pillai secured a certificate of fitness under Art. 134(1)(c). The Supreme Court allowed the appeal of A. K. Gopalan and dismissed the appeal of P. Govinda Pillai. The fine, if already paid by A. K. Gopalan, shall be refunded. The Supreme Court maintained the conviction entered by the High Court against the appellant P. Govinda Pillai.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal of A. K. Gopalan is allowed and the appeal of P. Govinda Pillai is dismissed.
decision.conviction_status: The conviction entered by the High Court against the appellant P. Govinda Pillai is maintained.
directions: The fine, if already paid by A. K. Gopalan, shall be refunded.

issue.issue_text: Whether the first appellant, A. K. Gopalan, was guilty of contempt of court for making the statement complained of.

facts: The first appellant, A. K. Gopalan, made a statement on September 20, 1967.
An arrest related to the incident was made on September 23, 1967.
The statement was published in a newspaper on September 25, 1967.
law: For a statement to constitute contempt of court, it must be made when legal proceedings are either pending or imminent.
application: The Court determined that the relevant date for assessing A. K. Gopalan's liability was September 20, 1967, the day he made the statement, not the day it was published.
The Court found that there was no evidence to prove that any court proceedings were imminent on September 20, 1967.
reasoning.conclusion: In a majority opinion, the Supreme Court decided that A. K. Gopalan was not guilty of contempt of court because there was no evidence that any court proceedings were imminent on the date he made the statement. Consequently, his conviction by the High Court was overturned.

issue.issue_text: Whether the second appellant, P. Govinda Pillai, was guilty of contempt of court for publishing the statement in the newspaper.

facts: A person was killed in a clash, and a First Information Report was lodged on September 11, 1967.
The accused were arrested on September 23, 1967, in connection with the death.
On September 24, 1967, a Magistrate remanded the accused to police custody.
P. Govinda Pillai, the second appellant and editor of the 'Deshabhimani' newspaper, published a statement about the case on September 25, 1967.
law: Contempt of court can be committed by publishing a comment that is likely to prejudice the due course of justice.
This rule applies not only to proceedings that are already pending but also to proceedings that are 'imminent'.
application: The Court examined whether legal proceedings were 'imminent' on September 25, 1967, the date the statement was published.

It reasoned that since the accused had already been arrested two days prior for a serious cognizable offense and had been produced before a magistrate who authorized their detention, court proceedings were indeed imminent.
The Court noted that the arrest and remand by a magistrate indicated that the case was on a clear path toward the courts.

It rejected the argument that proceedings are only imminent once the police file a final report, stating that such a rule would harm the accused by encouraging public investigation and discussion while the official investigation is ongoing.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because court proceedings were imminent at the time of publication, P. Govinda Pillai was guilty of contempt of court. Therefore, it maintained the conviction and dismissed his appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the first appellant, A. K. Gopalan, was guilty of contempt of court for making the statement complained of.
appellant_arguments: The relevant date for determining contempt is September 20, the day the statement was made, not the day it was published.
On the date the statement was made, there was no evidence that any judicial proceedings were pending or imminent.
The lodging of a First Information Report does not by itself establish that proceedings in a court were imminent.
There is no evidence that the first appellant was instrumental in getting the statement published on September 25.
respondent_arguments: The crucial date is September 25, when the newspaper published the statement, not September 20.
Given that a First Information Report for a serious crime had been lodged, it is not possible to hold that proceedings were not imminent on September 20.
The first appellant knew or had reason to believe that court proceedings were imminent when he made the statement.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the second appellant, P. Govinda Pillai, was guilty of contempt of court for publishing the statement in the newspaper.
appellant_arguments: The provided text does not explicitly state the second appellant's arguments.
respondent_arguments: The crucial date for the publisher is the date of publication, September 25.
By the date of publication, the accused had already been arrested (September 23) and remanded to custody by a Magistrate (September 24), meaning judicial proceedings were clearly pending or imminent.

cases.case_name: Case cited as [1927] I K. B. 845 at 851
cases.principle: The jurisdiction to punish for contempt of court is not confined to cases where, at the moment of publication, there is a cause actually pending in the High Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction for contempt of court based on a publication cannot be sustained if, at the time the offending article was published, no judicial proceeding was pending or imminent.
obiter: It is common knowledge that whenever a man loses his life, an investigation is bound to follow and a prosecution is not a distant possibility.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court distinguished liability for contempt of court based on the specific act and its timing. The first appellant, who made the statement, was not guilty because at the time he spoke, judicial proceedings were not considered imminent, as the mere lodging of a First Information Report is insufficient to establish imminence. However, the second appellant, who published the statement later, was found guilty because by the date of publication, the accused had been arrested and remanded, making judicial proceedings imminent and the publication an act calculated to prejudice a fair trial.
legal_tests_applied: The essence of the offence of contempt is conduct calculated to produce an atmosphere of prejudice in the midst of which the proceedings will have to go on and a tendency to interfere with the due course of justice or to prejudice mankind against persons who are on trial or who may be brought to trial.
A person is guilty of contempt if, 'knowing or having good reason to believe that criminal proceedings are imminent, he chooses to publish matters calculated to prejudice a fair trial.'
For contempt to be established, it must be shown that at the time of the publication or statement, a judicial proceeding was pending or imminent.
The lodging of a First Information Report does not by itself establish that proceedings in a court were imminent.
why_appellant_lost: The crucial date for determining contempt for the publisher (the second appellant) is the date of publication, not the date the statement was originally made.
By the date the second appellant published the statement, judicial proceedings were imminent or pending, as the accused had already been arrested and remanded to custody by a Magistrate.
Publishing a statement that tends to 'prejudice mankind against the accused' when proceedings are imminent constitutes contempt because it has a tendency to interfere with the due course of justice.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the publisher's liability is judged at the time of publication.
The respondent established that by the time of publication, the arrest and remand of the accused meant judicial proceedings were no longer a mere possibility but were imminent or pending.
The respondent demonstrated that the published statement was of a nature calculated to create an atmosphere of prejudice, which is the essence of the offense.
policy_considerations: The power to punish for contempt is 'wide' and 'arbitrary' and therefore 'must be exercised with circumspection, carefully and with restraint and only in cases where it is necessary for maintaining the course of justice pure and unaffected.'
The law of contempt must be used to 'preserve citizens' right to have a fair trial of their causes and proceedings in an atmosphere free of all prejudice or prepossession.'
It would be an 'undue restriction on the liherty of free speech to lay down that even before any arrest has been made there should be no comments on the facts of a particular case.'
In some cases, 'it is the duty of a free press to comment on such topics so as to bring them to the attention of the public,' especially in matters of public scandal.
